        Buildout

        Research desk, not investment advice. The model book is illustrative. Scenario sizes and tool inputs are assumptions; every market figure links to its source and date.

        Decision engine

        From 156 years of data to a sized exposure, gated by its own record

          Inference

          Regime state and changepoint probability

          A hidden Markov model reads monthly real returns as draws from a few regimes, each with its own mean and volatility, that persist and switch. The engine refits it every five years with the number of states chosen by BIC and reads each month's regime odds forward only (filtered), so no decision ever used the future. Bayesian online changepoint detection asks a separate question: how long has the current regime lasted?

          Odds of the stressed regime
          The regimes today

          Shrunk means pull each state toward the long-run mean with 120 months of prior, so a regime seen rarely does not size the book. Volatility is annualized.

          Chance a new regime began in the last six months

          Models

          Model weights and their basis

          Two layers of averaging, both scored only on what was already known. The return density for next month averages the regime model, the changepoint model, the long-run average and the geometric-analog model by their recent predictive likelihood (2% forgetting a month). The analog model reads the 12 months after the 8 past windows whose stock-bond covariance is nearest today's; a placebo on the Geometry desk shows its gain comes from mixing several pasts, not from the resemblance. The 12-month view stacks four forecasters with non-negative weights fit on their earlier out-of-sample errors; it tilts the monthly mean.

          Return-density models, weight today
          Their weights through history
          The 12-month forecasters, out of sample since 1940

          Scores differ slightly from the ML lab's: this run refits every 24 months on the decision engine's feature set; the lab refits every 12 on its own.

          Decision

          Exposure drivers and flip points

          The engine picks the exposure from 0 to 1.5x that maximizes expected utility of next month's wealth under the averaged mixture, with constant relative risk aversion set once, on 1871 to 1939 data, so that holding 1x is optimal in an average month. A risk budget caps the average loss across the worst 5% of months at 12% of capital (the 95% one-month expected shortfall, a model estimate and not a worst case). Then the evidence gate scales the move away from 1x by how much the engine's own past departures helped.

              The railway test

              What one year of AI capex must earn, against what the clouds bill

              In the 1840s British railway mania, investors had public traffic data, and share prices still implied four times the revenue the lines went on to earn (about £60m implied against about £15m actual in 1852; Odlyzko, 2010). The same test today: take one year of capex, ask what revenue it must generate to pay back its depreciation and earn its cost of capital, and set that against what the three clouds bill. The defaults are sourced; move them.

              Sources: capex guides after Q3 2026 (Microsoft about $170B for calendar 2026, Amazon about $220B, Alphabet $195 to 205B, Meta $135 to 145B; midpoints used); Q3 2026 cloud revenue (AWS $46.0B, Google Cloud $30.7B, Microsoft Cloud $63.9B, which includes commercial Office); 36% is Google Cloud's Q3 operating margin; the 3-year life is the IMF's stress case (GFSR, April 2026). The test covers one vintage only: the 2024 and 2025 spending also has to earn its return out of the same revenue.

              Earnings quality

              Mark-to-market gains on cross-holdings

              Non-operating income is mostly gains on stakes in other AI companies. It counts in earnings per share, it is reflexive (it rises with the boom), and it reverses faster than the business.

              The depreciation wave

              Future depreciation from current capital expenditure

              Capex hits the income statement later, as depreciation. The model below is fitted to each company's reported depreciation, then run forward on its guidance, at the stated server life and at a shorter one.

              The modelEach year's capex Cv enters service mid-year; a share s depreciates over the server life Ls, the rest over 25 years. Dt = ∑v Cv [ s·overlap(t, v, Ls)/Ls + (1 − s)·overlap(t, v, 25)/25 ]. s is solved so the model reproduces the reported depreciation in the fit year. Land and construction in progress are not separated, so the wave arrives later than modeled.

              System

              Engine architecture, conventions and status

              Python, about 33,000 lines of engine code and 70 test files, run every weekday on GitHub Actions. One timing rule runs through all of it: a value at date t uses data through the close of t, and a decision made at t earns returns from t+1.

              The five stages of the daily run

              1. Data

                99 sources: FRED curve, credit, volatility, oil, inflation, jobs, sentiment and financial conditions daily; feeds from Substack, Telegram, X, Reddit and the wires; SEC 10-K and 10-Q facts; 156 years of public data monthly; Databento bars with split and dividend factors; Kalshi odds.

              2. Exposures

                Daily betas to market, AI and rates factors. SPCX leans on TSLA's betas until it has its own history.

              3. Regime

                Stock-bond correlation, exponentially weighted with a 63-day half-life, read with hysteresis: hedging, neutral or amplifying.

              4. Hedge & size

                Min-variance TLT ratio when the regime allows it. Vol target and drawdown cap set gross; Kelly checks the edge.

              5. Prove

                Dollar-exact backtest with costs and financing, deflated Sharpe, and walk-forward forecasts judged on calibration.

              v0.7 · the policy contract

              Policies and conventions

              Every displayed decision names the policy that made it, and the engine backtests the same function. These are the specifications and the accounting conventions every performance number follows.

              hedge.tlt.v2

              Hold TLT at the minimum-variance ratio (capped at 1.0x) only while the stock-bond state is "hedging" and, when the research has a validated inflation line, 36-month inflation is below it. The state enters at a correlation of −0.10 or below and leaves only above 0. A missing input makes the decision unavailable.

              size.equity.v2

              Equity scale = the smallest of the volatility target over forecast volatility, the one-year 25% drawdown cap (95% confidence, simulated) and 1.5x. Quarter Kelly is reported beside it as an edge check, never as a size input.

              limits.portfolio.v1

              After the hedge is added, equity plus bond notional may not exceed 2.0x NAV; option premium is capped at 2% of NAV. Equity and hedge scale down together when the cap binds.

              Accounting

              One NAV series: costs and financing come out of NAV the day they occur, the first trade's cost is in the first return, and the product of returns equals final NAV. Signals at the close of day t trade at the close of t+1. Sharpe is in excess of the cash actually accrued.

              Comparisons

              Every variant runs on the same dates after the warm-up, from the same starting NAV, beside an unhedged book and a cash-only baseline. The deflated Sharpe counts every variant, hedge policy and candidate hedge tried.

              Concentration

              Effective risk contributors (1 ÷ Σ risk share²) measures concentration by position. Effective independent bets (Meucci, across principal components) measures how many drivers the risk loads on. Two equal, perfectly correlated positions score 2 and 1.

              The engine · in plain English

              How the engine decides, in one sentence, one paragraph and one page

              No jargon on this desk. Every term the other desks use is defined here in a line, and any month since 1940 can be replayed to watch the engine make its call from the data it had at the time.

              On this deskOne sentenceOne paragraphSix stagesReplay a monthThe wordsWhat it is not

              In one sentence

              What the engine does every month

              Every month the engine reads 156 years of market data, works out what kind of market this is, estimates what the next year is likely to pay, chooses how much stock a cautious investor would hold given that, and then trusts its own answer only as far as its track record since 1940 has earned.

              In one paragraph

              The same thing, with the moving parts named

              The engine is a set of numbers learned from history, with the rules that update them written down in advance. It starts from monthly US stock returns since 1871 and a handful of things known at the time: how expensive stocks are, where bond yields and inflation stand, how the market has been trending, how volatile it has been and how far it sits below its last high. From these it keeps two kinds of belief up to date. One is about the state of the market: a few regimes (calm, turbulent, stressed), each with its own typical return and risk, and the odds of being in each this month. The other is about the next year: four simple forecasters, combined by how well each has actually done.

              It then asks one question. For an investor who dislikes losses about as much as the average long-run investor must have (the dislike is set so that holding exactly one times capital is the neutral answer), what exposure to stocks makes the next month's expected outcome best, provided the average loss across the worst 5% of months is no more than 12% of capital? That number is the engine's optimum, 1.50x today.

              Between that optimum and the book sits a gate. The engine moves the book away from plain holding only in proportion to how strong its own record since 1940 is, after discounting for every version of itself that was tried. Today that record is not strong enough, so the gate is 0% and the engine holds the index at 1.00x; the book's own risk limits, measured on its nine names, then cut it (the Desk shows the size). Two standing guards sit alongside: a hedge selector that chooses between all stocks, a Treasury sleeve and a cash sleeve by their recent record in the current regime, and a trend overlay that would scale exposure when the market is below its 10-month average, adopted only if the scaling survives the same walk-forward test the engine applies to itself. Today the overlay is tested and not adopted, because it failed the same walk-forward test the engine applies to itself.

              Six stages

              The engine as a weather service

              A weather service does not promise tomorrow's rain. It reads its instruments, names the season, publishes an outlook with its uncertainty, and tells you whether to carry an umbrella. The engine has the same six jobs.

              1Data: the instruments

              156 years of monthly readings, each dated. A value for month t uses data through t minus two, so nothing is used before it could have been known.

              What can go wrong: a stale feed. The engine says which date each number carries and marks anything older than its schedule.

              The rulea value used in month t is fit on data through t − 2 (LAG = 2); refits: regimes every 60 months, forecasters every 24, the learner every 12.
              Engine room →
              2Regimes: the season

              Not "will it rain tomorrow" but "is this a stormy season": the odds of calm, turbulent and stressed markets this month, from a model refit every five years, plus a check for whether a new season has just begun.

              What can go wrong: regimes are labels fitted after the fact. The engine averages four different views of the next month by how well each has recently predicted it, so no single label decides.

              The modelst ~ Markov(A), rt | st = k ~ N(μk, σk2); filter αt ∝ (αt−1A) ⊙ p(rt | s); state means shrunk: μ̃k = r̄ + nk/(nk + n0)(μk − r̄).
              The states today →
              3Forecasts: the outlook

              Four forecasters of the next year's return, each refit every two years and combined by their record. The outlook carries its own uncertainty, which is wide.

              What can go wrong: forecasting returns is barely possible. Out of sample, the best forecaster only edges the long-run average; the engine's edge is in the budget and the discipline, not the forecast.

              The combinationf = Σj vj fj, v = argmin Στ < t−12 (yτ − Σj vjfj,τ)2, v ≥ 0, Σv = 1 (stacking on forecasts whose outcomes were known).
              The forecasters' record →
              4Allocation: the umbrella

              How much stock to carry: the exposure with the best expected outcome for a cautious investor, inside a budget of 12% of capital for the average loss in the worst 5% of months.

              What can go wrong: the budget binds in a storm and the engine cuts exposure late. That is accepted; the budget is a mandate's limit, not a forecast.

              The choicex* = argmax0 ≤ x ≤ 1.5 E[(v1−γ − 1)/(1 − γ)], v = 1 + xR − b max(x − 1, 0), subject to x·ES5%(R) ≤ 12%.
              The sizing math →
              5Gate: how far to trust the forecaster

              A forecaster who has not beaten "assume tomorrow looks like today" gets little say. The gate scales the move from holding toward the optimum by the strength of the engine's own record, discounted for every version tried.

              What can go wrong: a gate that someone can tune. This one cannot: it is a fixed function of the record's t statistic and the count of strategies tried.

              The gateg = max(0, 2Φ(t − t0) − 1), t0 = Φ−1(1 − 1/n), x = 1 + g(x* − 1).
              The gate today →
              6Hedge and overlay: the standing guards

              What to hold beside the stocks (all stocks, a Treasury sleeve or cash, chosen by recent record in the current regime), and the rule that scales exposure when the trend breaks.

              What can go wrong: bonds stop hedging when inflation is high, which is the case now, and a rule that looks free on the full record can fail when re-chosen year by year, which is what happened to the trend overlay. The selector holds no bond sleeve and the overlay is not applied.

              The selectorP(h best | context) estimated by Thompson draws from discounted outcome means (forgetting 0.995); the overlay factor f is kept only if, re-chosen each year on the record to date, E[u] is at least holding’s.

              The words

              Eight terms the other desks use, one line each

              Regime
              A stretch of months that share a typical return and risk. The engine fits a few and keeps the odds of being in each.
              Forecast
              A guess at the next year's real return, with its uncertainty. Four of them, combined by record.
              Risk aversion
              How much more a loss hurts than a gain helps. Set so that holding one times capital is the neutral answer; not tuned.
              Expected shortfall
              The average loss across the worst 5% of months the model expects, over one month. It is an average of the tail, so single months inside it are worse; it is not a worst case and not a one-month-in-twenty event (that cutoff is the value at risk). The engine keeps it under 12% of capital.
              Optimum
              The exposure with the best expected outcome for that risk aversion inside that budget. Today 1.50x.
              Gate
              The share of the move from holding toward the optimum that reaches the book, from the strength of the record. Today 0%.
              Overlay
              A scaling of exposure when the market is below its 10-month average. Adopted only if it keeps a cautious investor's expected utility walked forward; today none is.
              Walked forward
              Every number for a past month was computed only from data available then, so the record is a fair test of the fitted parameters; the design choices (which models, the hand-set constants) were made knowing the history.

              Limits

              What the engine is not

              Not a price predictor

              Its forecasters barely beat the long-run average out of sample, and it says so. The value is in the risk budget, the regime odds, the gate and the written-down rules, not in calling the market.

              What can and cannot send an order

              Nothing on this site places, routes or cancels a trade, and the MCP server has no order tool: both write proposals a person approves. The trader is a separate program in the same repository. It trades a public paper account on its own, and on a person's machine it can reach a broker under a signed, armed mandate (Execution).

              Not tuned

              Eleven constants are set by hand and listed with reasons; the gate is a fixed function of the record once the count of strategies tried is fixed; the overlay factor was chosen by a rule stated before the result and then rejected by that rule's own walk-forward. No parameter was tuned to the backtest's result, though the design was chosen knowing the history.

              Not a black box

              Twenty-two learned objects, 2,850 numbers in the decision core, each with its shape and its optimiser on the Parameters desk; the source is on the source desk; the daily record is the Engine room.

                    Today · from the call to orders

                    The call becomes a ticket; which system may send it, and on whose approval

                    Buildout decides what to trade and whether it is allowed. This page and Buildout's research server place no orders and hold no brokerage credential. The trader, a separate program, can: it runs a public paper account on its own from the daily run, and on a person's own machine it can reach a Robinhood Agentic account under a signed mandate. The table says which system can send what.

                    Capabilities

                    Who can send an order, to which account, on whose approval

                    Four systems share this code. Only the last two can reach a real account, and neither is set up by the public repository: the mandate and any credential live in a private folder that is never committed, so this page cannot read their state and does not claim one.

                    The flow

                    The assistant route: five steps, two servers, one approval

                    1. The call is logged. The day's size and hedge are written to the hash-chained ledger before the next trading day (ledger/calls.jsonl).
                    2. Robinhood is read. The assistant reads the Agentic account (equity, cash, positions) and quotes through Robinhood's Trading MCP.
                    3. Buildout writes the ticket. trade_plan turns the call into target holdings and limit orders, runs every check below, and returns a hashed ticket id that expires in 15 minutes.
                    4. A person approves. Nothing is placed unless every check passes, the account is in live mode, and the person approves that exact ticket id.
                    5. Robinhood places; Buildout records. Each order goes through Robinhood's MCP as a limit order, sells first; record_fills checks the fills against the ticket and chains them into a private log.

                    What the account allows

                    The call, mapped to what a Robinhood Agentic account can hold

                    Today's targets

                    Share of the account in each holding, both variants

                    The checks

                    Every ticket, every time

                    The trader · v0.42

                    From the recommendation to orders, under a mandate, in one of three modes

                    The trader is a separate program (python -m buildout trader) that can act for a person. Each pass runs the same way whatever the mode: is trading halted, is it inside the window, has it already acted today; read the account and quotes from the broker; build the ticket (the planner above, every check); check the ticket against the mandate's limits; then the mode decides whether it waits for a person or goes. Execution is sells first, buys from the proceeds, each order polled to its fill or cancelled at the ticket's expiry; the fills go to the hash-chained log; the account is marked; a journal line and a digest are written. One ticket a day, one order per id, the ticket's id covering every field: a pass can be repeated without repeating a trade.

                    The three modes
                    Three routes to the market

                    The mandate

                    The terms the person writes and signs

                    A small file (private/mandate.toml, never committed) that nothing in Buildout can write. Its hash goes into every ticket and journal line, so a change of terms shows in the record. Nothing trades for real until it says armed = true over a name and a date, and an armed autonomous mandate has to say in its notes why unattended trading is wanted. The limits below are the template's defaults.

                    Run it

                    Paper first, then supervised, then autonomous

                    git clone https://github.com/jamesplacco/buildout && cd buildout
python -m buildout trader --init          # mandate.toml and broker.toml templates in private/; edit, sign
python -m buildout trader --once          # one pass (mode and broker from the mandate; paper by default)
python -m buildout trader --approve tkt-… # manual, supervised: approve a staged ticket
python -m buildout trader --loop 15       # a pass every 15 minutes in the window, until private/HALT

claude                                    # assistant route: Buildout's MCP plus Robinhood's Trading MCP
/rebalance                                # trading_recommendation: account in, mandate decides, assistant places

python -m buildout broker probe           # direct route: list Robinhood's tools; fill private/broker.toml
python -m buildout broker login           # sign in once; tokens stay in private/
python -m buildout trade halt             # the kill switch, every route

                    Tickets, fills, approvals, the journal and the mandate live in private/, which git ignores: nothing about a real account reaches this page or the repository. The paper bot's state lives in paper/, committed, because it is a model account.

                    The engine · parameters

                    Θ: every matrix the engine learns, and what shaped it

                    The engine is one system whose parameters are numerical matrices, vectors and scalars shaped by optimisation: transition matrices by expectation-maximisation, regression weights by penalised least squares, network weights by Adam with early stopping, a Q-table by fitted Q-iteration, model weights by discounted Bayesian updating, a causal skeleton by a graphical lasso, and a knowledge graph compressed to 64 numbers a node by an eigendecomposition. This desk is the inventory: what has been learned, how much, by which algorithm against which objective, on what data, refit how often, and feeding which desks. The few constants chosen by judgment are listed apart, each with its reason.

                    On this deskThe layersThe inventorySet by handHow to read it

                    The layers

                    Eight layers, in the order data flows through them

                      The inventory

                      Every learned object: shape, count, optimiser, objective, data, refit, destination

                      Select a row for its data, its as-of date, today's values and the module that fits it. Counts are the numbers the engine multiplies, not free parameters: a 3 by 3 transition matrix counts nine although six are free.

                      Set by hand

                      Constants chosen by judgment, with their reasons

                      Not fitted to outcomes. Each one is a choice a reviewer can disagree with, so each carries the reason it was made and where it acts. Changing one reruns the engine; nothing else on the site hides a dial.

                      How to read it

                      Why the decision core is small, and why that is the point

                      Learned against set

                      A parameter is learned when an algorithm chose its value to optimise a stated objective on stated data; it is set when a person chose it. The engine keeps the two apart because they fail differently: a learned value drifts with the data and is caught by the refit schedule and the walk-forward record; a set value is a judgment and is caught only by a reader who disagrees. Every row above says which it is.

                      Why so few numbers decide

                      The decision core is a few thousand numbers because the targets are noisy and the history, though long, is one history. Each forecaster is refit every two years on a few hundred effective observations; a model with many more parameters than that would fit the noise, which is what the machine-learning lab finds when it tries. The one large object, the knowledge graph's spectral map, is not a forecast: it compresses what the system knows so that every question becomes a matrix product, and it is judged by retrieval, not by returns.

                      Walked forward, with a lag

                      A value used at month t was fit on data through t minus two. The refit schedule is part of the parameter: the regime models refit every five years (eighteen fits since 1940), the forecasters every two, the recursive objects every month. The gate then decides how much of the engine's optimum reaches the book, from the t statistic of its record against the best of eight useless strategies.

                      Where to look

                      The inventory is produced by buildout/parameters.py from the engines' own outputs, so it cannot disagree with the run. python -m buildout parameters prints it; the MCP tool parameter_inventory serves it by layer or by object; the source desk shows every module named in the table. The mind carries each object as a node, so a question about the engine's weights is answered from the same inventory.
